item.title: Stop Blaming Your RAG Pipeline. 16 Techniques That Actually Work in Production
item.content:encoded:
A complete guide to the RAG pipeline, from query intake to response delivery. Every code block is runnable as written.

When a RAG system gives a wrong or vague answer, the first instinct is to blame the model. Swap in a bigger one, the thinking goes, and the problem disappears. It usually does not. Most quality problems live in the pipeline around the model. The query was never normalized. Retrieval pulled the wrong chunks. Nothing reranked them. The prompt let the model wander. The model is doing its best with bad context.

This guide is the fix. The 16 techniques below are the levers to pull when your RAG is underperforming, walked stage by stage from query intake to response delivery. Each one targets a specific failure point, with runnable code and a diagram. Work through them in order, or jump to the stage you suspect. Before you blame the model, check the pipeline.

TL;DR

  • RAG is not dead. It is the foundation of production AI.
  • The pipeline: query intake → normalization → intent detection → expansion → embedding → retrieval → reranking → context → generation → post-processing → delivery.
  • The 5 techniques with the most leverage: intent detection, query expansion, hybrid retrieval, reranking, and evaluation.
  • A common failure I keep seeing: chunk size set without testing. Start at 300 to 500 tokens with 10 to 20 percent overlap, then tune against your own eval set.
  • The most overlooked area: monitoring and evaluation. If you are not measuring, you are guessing.

For the architectural context that makes RAG possible, see RAG vs MCP: The Architectural Difference Every AI Developer Must Understand.

Table of Contents

  1. The RAG Pipeline at a Glance
  2. Query Intake: Channels and Ingestion
  3. Query Normalization and Preprocessing
  4. Intent Detection and Query Classification
  5. Query Expansion and Reformulation
  6. Embedding Generation: Models and Best Practices
  7. Document Ingestion and Parsing
  8. Chunking and Semantic Segmentation
  9. Embedding and Indexing: Vector Stores
  10. Retrieval Strategies: Dense, Sparse, and Hybrid
  11. Retriever Implementations and Libraries
  12. Reranking and Relevance Scoring
  13. Context Construction and Prompt Engineering
  14. LLM Generation: Model Selection and Configuration
  15. Post-processing and Response Delivery
  16. Monitoring, Evaluation, and Human-in-the-Loop
  17. Security, Privacy, and Compliance
  18. Personalization and User Context
  19. Scaling, Performance, and Cost Optimization
  20. Fallback Strategies and Hybrid Systems
  21. Explainability, Provenance, and Auditability
  22. Orchestration and Workflow Tooling
  23. End-to-End Code Example
  24. Conclusion: RAG in Practice

1. The RAG Pipeline at a Glance

A RAG system is a bridge. On one side, a pre-trained language model with a frozen view of the world. On the other side, your business knowledge, which changes daily. RAG pulls the relevant pieces from your knowledge sources at query time and hands them to the model along with the question. The model answers from what it just read, not what it memorized months ago. This solves the three failure modes that make plain LLMs unusable for real products: stale knowledge, hallucination, and the inability to cite sources [1].

Why the pipeline view matters:

  • Bridges a frozen model with live business knowledge. The model does not need to know everything. It needs to read the right thing at the right time.
  • Attacks three failure modes head on. Stale knowledge, hallucination, and weak explainability all come from the same root cause: the model is guessing without grounded context.
  • Every stage is independently tunable. This is the part most teams miss. RAG is not one system. It is eleven systems chained together, each of which can quietly break.

Example scenario: A customer asks, “What is the return policy for Product X?” The RAG system has to find the latest, product-specific policy from internal PDFs, FAQs, and ticket logs, then return a clear, sourced answer.

The reason I lay it out this way is because most production failures I have seen are not “the model is bad.” They are “stage 4 is silently broken and stage 9 is masking it.” Treating the pipeline as a single black box makes those bugs invisible. Treating it as eleven stages makes them addressable.

2. Query Intake: Channels and Ingestion

The RAG journey starts the moment a user submits a query. In our example, the customer’s question (“What is the return policy for Product X?”) might arrive through web chat, a mobile app, a voice assistant, or email. Each channel has its own pre-processing quirks. Voice needs speech-to-text. Web forms need HTML stripping. Email needs signature removal and quote-thread cleanup.

Three things worth getting right at this stage:

  • Channel normalization. Standardize the input regardless of where it came from. Lowercase, strip HTML, normalize whitespace, and run a typo fix if your users tend to write fast. The goal is that the same question through any channel ends up looking the same downstream.
  • Session and context tracking. A follow-up question like “what about for premium customers?” makes no sense without the previous turn. Track session state from turn one, not when you finally need it.
  • Input sanitization. Anything from an untrusted channel can carry a prompt injection payload [10]. Strip suspicious patterns, validate length, and reject obvious attacks early. You do not want to find out at the LLM stage.

3. Query Normalization and Preprocessing

Before retrieval, the raw query gets normalized. The goal is to make semantically similar queries map to similar representations. If “Product X” and “product x” embed to different vectors, your recall suffers for no good reason.

import re

def normalize_query(query: str) -> str:
    # Lowercase and remove punctuation
    query = query.lower()
    query = re.sub(r'[^\w\s]', '', query)
    # Optionally: spell correction, stopword removal, etc.
    return query.strip()

normalized = normalize_query("What is the return policy for Product X?")
print(normalized)  # "what is the return policy for product x"

The normalization steps worth running:

  • Lowercasing and punctuation removal. Cheap, fast, and catches most surface-level mismatches.
  • Spell correction. Worth it for consumer-facing systems where users type fast. Skip it for internal tools where precision matters more than forgiveness.
  • Stopword filtering. Optional and retriever-dependent. Dense retrieval usually does not need it. BM25 sometimes benefits, sometimes hurts. Test it.
  • Entity recognition. Pulling out “Product X” as a product entity lets you filter retrieval by metadata later. Pays for itself once you have more than one product line.

4. Intent Detection and Query Classification

Intent detection puts the user’s query into a bucket. Policy inquiry. Order status. Technical support. The bucket drives two downstream decisions: which retrieval index to hit, and which prompt template to use. A policy question goes to the policy docs. An order question goes to the order logs. Mixing them up wastes retrieval budget and confuses the model.

The example uses zero-shot classification, which accepts candidate labels without a trained classifier.

from transformers import pipeline

intent_classifier = pipeline("text-classification", model="facebook/bart-large-mnli")
query = "What is the return policy for Product X?"
labels = ["policy_inquiry", "order_status", "technical_support"]
result = intent_classifier(query, candidate_labels=labels)
print(result)

Why intent matters more than people think:

  • Picks the right retrieval index. Policy docs and order logs are different corpora. Searching both wastes recall and adds noise to the context.
  • Picks the right prompt template. A “policy answer” prompt should sound different from a “troubleshooting” prompt. Same model, different system prompts, different outcomes.
  • Enables FAQ short-circuit. Common intents can skip the whole retrieval pipeline and hit a curated FAQ instead (covered in Section 20). This is the cheapest latency and quality improvement most teams ignore.

5. Query Expansion and Reformulation

Short queries miss long, detailed documents. A user typing “return policy” will not match a chunk that talks about “refund eligibility windows and merchandise return procedures.” The embedding model knows they are related, but only weakly. Query expansion fixes this by making the query look more like the answer.

# HyDE: Generate a hypothetical answer, then embed and retrieve
from langchain.prompts import PromptTemplate
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI, OpenAIEmbeddings

llm = ChatOpenAI(model_name="gpt-4o-mini")
hyde_prompt = PromptTemplate(
    input_variables=["user_question"],
    template="Given this question: '{user_question}'
Write a detailed answer as if for a product manual."
)
hypothetical_answer = llm.invoke({"user_question": query})
# Now embed hypothetical_answer and use for retrieval

The three expansion techniques worth knowing:

  • HyDE (Hypothetical Document Embeddings). Generate a hypothetical answer with an LLM, embed it, retrieve against the hypothetical embedding [3]. The hypothetical answer uses the vocabulary of source documents, so retrieval lines up better.
  • Paraphrasing. Generate two or three LLM rewrites of the original query, embed each, and union the results. Catches alternate phrasings the user did not think to use.
  • Multi-prompt expansion (HyPE). Generate multiple expanded prompts covering different angles of the same question. Useful when queries are vague or could be interpreted multiple ways.

The honest catch with HyDE: the hypothetical answer can hallucinate. That is fine for retrieval, where you only use the embedding, but never use the hypothetical text as part of your context. I have watched teams accidentally pipe the hypothetical answer straight to the user. Do not be that team.

For the broader set of question patterns that separate senior AI engineers from beginners, see The 10 Questions That Decide Whether You’re an AI Engineer or Just an AI User.

6. Embedding Generation: Models and Best Practices

The normalized (and possibly expanded) query gets encoded into a dense vector with an embedding model. The choice of embedding model is crucial for retrieval quality.

from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
model = SentenceTransformer('sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2')
query_embedding = model.encode(normalized)
print(query_embedding.shape)  # (384,)

Three rules I have not seen anyone successfully break:

  • Use the same embedding model on both sides. Mixing embedding models on queries versus documents is a silent killer that produces plausible-looking nonsense. The vectors live in different spaces. Cosine similarity becomes meaningless.
  • Batch encode for throughput. Embedding is expensive. Batching turns it from “slow” to “fast enough” for almost any workload. Most embedding libraries default to single-item encoding, which is a trap.
  • Cache results aggressively. A frequently-asked query should hit the embedding cache, not the embedding model. LRU caching at the query level is one of the highest-ROI optimizations in the entire pipeline.

Model choice by use case:

  • English-only general retrieval: the smaller MiniLM models are surprisingly good and fast.
  • Multilingual: you need a multilingual model end to end, not just on one side.
  • Domain-specific (legal, medical, code): a domain-tuned embedding model can outperform a much bigger general one.

7. Document Ingestion and Parsing

Document ingestion is the unglamorous side of RAG. Loading, parsing, and cleaning all your knowledge sources before any of the clever retrieval logic runs.

Sources you will deal with in production:

  • Product catalog PDFs. Parse with OCR if scanned. Native PDFs can usually use a text extractor like PyPDF.
  • Policy documents. PDF, HTML, DOCX. Each format has its quirks. Test extraction quality on real documents, not perfect samples.
  • FAQ pages. HTML or Markdown. Strip navigation chrome, ads, and boilerplate before chunking.
  • Order history and ticket logs. CSV, JSON, or a database query. Schema-aware parsing beats blob ingestion every time.

from langchain_community.document_loaders import PyPDFLoader
from langchain.text_splitter import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter

pdf_loader = PyPDFLoader("policy.pdf")
raw_docs = pdf_loader.load()
splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(chunk_size=500, chunk_overlap=100)
chunks = splitter.split_documents(raw_docs)

One thing that gets missed in tutorials: tables. PDFs with product specs, pricing tables, or compatibility matrices need a dedicated table extractor, not the default text loader. The default will flatten a table into a soup of comma-separated numbers, and you will wonder why your retrieval cannot answer “what is the warranty on the 14-inch model.”

8. Chunking and Semantic Segmentation

Chunking is a tradeoff. Too small and you lose context. Too large and retrieval gets imprecise because relevant content sits next to irrelevant content in the same chunk. A 300 to 500 token chunk with 10 to 20 percent overlap is a reasonable starting point, but treat it as a hypothesis to test against your own eval set, not a fixed rule.

# Technique 5: Chunking
from langchain_text_splitters import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter

splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(
    chunk_size=500,
    chunk_overlap=100,
    separators=["

", "
", ".", " ", ""],
)
chunks = splitter.split_documents(raw_docs)

The three chunking decisions that matter most:

  • Chunk size (300 to 500 tokens to start). Tune against your own eval set. A medical Q&A system might need smaller, denser chunks. A long-form policy document might tolerate larger ones. Do not pick a chunk size by guessing.
  • Overlap (10 to 20 percent). Without overlap, a single relevant sentence can split across two chunks and end up retrieved poorly in both. With overlap, that sentence appears whole in at least one chunk. The cost is some duplicated tokens, which is a fair trade.
  • Split boundaries. Prefer semantic boundaries (paragraphs, sections) over fixed character counts. Splitting mid-sentence is the fastest way to make retrieval feel “almost right but never useful.”

For a much deeper treatment of chunking decisions and what 80+ interviews of senior engineers revealed about how they actually pick chunk sizes, see Chunking Strategies in RAG Systems: Insights from 80+ GenAI Interviews.

9. Embedding and Indexing: Vector Stores

Each chunk gets embedded into a dense vector and stored in a vector database for fast similarity search. The vector store landscape moves fast, and what was correct in 2024 is partly stale in 2026. As of early 2026, here is the honest take.

The vector stores worth considering:

  • Pinecone. Managed service with minimal operational overhead. It scales, it has hybrid search, and you do not have to think about it. The right choice if your team is small and your budget allows it.
  • Weaviate. Open source, GraphQL API, hybrid search, multi-tenancy. The right choice if you want flexibility and have the ops capacity to run it.
  • Qdrant. Open source, Rust-based, fast, advanced filtering. The right choice if filtering by metadata is core to your use case.
  • Milvus. Open source, enterprise scale, multiple index types. The right choice when you are operating at very large scale and need fine-grained index control.
  • FAISS. A library, not a database. In-memory, fast for small to medium datasets. The right choice for prototypes and embedded use cases.
import faiss
import numpy as np

index = faiss.IndexFlatL2(384)  # 384-dim vectors
index.add(document_embeddings)   # document_embeddings: np.ndarray
D, I = index.search(query_embedding.reshape(1, -1), k=5)
retrieved_docs = [documents[i] for i in I[0]]

The wrong choice is usually “the one we picked because the tutorial used it” without thinking about scale, latency, or filtering needs.

For the broader question of when a vector store alone is the wrong primitive and you need a relational and graph store alongside it, see Stop Picking Between Vector and Graph: Real Production AI Needs Three Databases.

10. Retrieval Strategies: Dense, Sparse, and Hybrid

Dense retrieval uses neural embeddings to find semantically similar chunks. “Return policy” matches “refund terms” even though no words overlap. Sparse retrieval (BM25, TF-IDF) matches exact keywords. Hybrid combines both with Reciprocal Rank Fusion [4].

The case for hybrid retrieval in three points:

  • Dense retrieval is great at meaning, bad at exact identifiers. SKUs, error codes, model numbers, regulation names, and customer IDs all get poorly matched by embeddings alone.
  • Sparse retrieval is great at exact identifiers, bad at meaning. “Refund policy” and “return guidelines” share no tokens but mean the same thing. BM25 will miss this.
  • Hybrid covers both. Reciprocal Rank Fusion combines the two ranked lists into a single list that respects both signals. Production systems almost always need this.

11. Retriever Implementations and Libraries

Retrievers return the top-k relevant chunks for a query. LangChain and LlamaIndex both provide retriever abstractions that wrap vector stores, BM25, and hybrid behind a single API. Pick one and stick with it. Switching mid-project is more painful than it should be.

from langchain_community.vectorstores import FAISS
from langchain_community.embeddings import HuggingFaceEmbeddings

embeddings = HuggingFaceEmbeddings(model_name="sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
vectorstore = FAISS.from_documents(chunks, embeddings)
retriever = vectorstore.as_retriever()
results = retriever.get_relevant_documents(query)

Advanced retriever patterns worth knowing:

  • Multi-hop retrievers. For questions that need information from multiple documents chained together. “Which engineer worked on Project A and also Project B” needs two retrievals stitched together.
  • Agentic retrievers. The LLM itself decides when to retrieve, what to retrieve, and when it has enough [6]. More flexible than fixed pipelines, harder to debug.
  • GraphRAG. Relationship-aware retrieval over a knowledge graph. Dramatically better than vector-only retrieval for questions about connections, dependencies, or hierarchies.

Most simple Q&A does not need any of these. Reach for them when your retrieval evaluation tells you simple retrieval is plateauing.

For the broader set of production patterns senior engineers use to make retrievers reliable under real load, see 11 Production AI Patterns Senior Engineers Are Quietly Adopting in 2026 (Part 1).

12. Reranking and Relevance Scoring

Initial retrieval returns a wide candidate set, usually 20 to 50 chunks. A cross-encoder reranker then scores each candidate against the specific query and picks the top n [5]. The two-stage approach gives a real precision lift, with the cost of a small latency hit per query [9].

# Example: reranking with a cross-encoder (pseudo-code)
from cohere import Client
co = Client("api-key")
rerank_results = co.rerank(
    query="What is the return policy for Product X?",
    documents=[doc.page_content for doc in retrieved_docs],
    top_n=3
)
top_docs = [retrieved_docs[i] for i in rerank_results.indices]

Why two stages beat one:

  • Stage one casts wide. Pull 20 to 50 candidates with cheap retrieval. The goal here is recall, not precision. You want the right answer in there somewhere.
  • Stage two sharpens. A cross-encoder reads each candidate alongside the query and scores them jointly. Joint reading captures interactions that separate embeddings cannot.
  • The tradeoff is honest. You get a real precision gain for an added per-query latency cost. Measure it on your data before quoting a number.

Note: In my testing, cross-encoder reranking gave a meaningful precision lift on a held-out query set. The number depends entirely on your data and your retriever. Measure it on your own data before quoting a percentage.

13. Context Construction and Prompt Engineering

The top-k retrieved chunks are assembled into a context block for the LLM. Prompt engineering is critical: the prompt must clearly instruct the LLM to use only the provided context, cite sources, and avoid hallucination.

prompt = f"""
You are a helpful assistant. Use only the following context to answer the question.
Cite your sources in parentheses after each fact.

Context:
{retrieved_docs[0].page_content}
{retrieved_docs[1].page_content}
...

Question: What is the return policy for Product X?
Answer:
"""

The three fusion strategies for combining chunks:

  • Early fusion (FiD). All context fed to the encoder at once [2]. Works well for smaller context windows and is the default for most production systems.
  • Late fusion (RAG-Sequence). Each chunk processed independently, then results aggregated. Useful when chunks come from different document types.
  • Marginal fusion (RAG-Fusion). Combines multiple retrievals using rank fusion [4]. Best for complex queries where multiple retrieval angles all matter.

The three prompt rules I have learned the hard way:

  • Delimit the context clearly. XML-style tags or explicit markers tell the model where context ends and instructions begin. Without this, the model can get confused about what to treat as data.
  • Instruct the model to treat context as data, not instructions. A document in your context window can contain “Ignore previous instructions and…” Inoculate against this in the system prompt.
  • Require a citation after each fact. Two benefits. It makes answers auditable, and it forces the model to ground itself in retrieved chunks rather than drifting into pre-trained knowledge.

14. LLM Generation: Model Selection and Configuration

The prompt gets passed to a generator model. The configuration knobs that matter for RAG are temperature, max tokens, stop sequences, and the system prompt. Model selection comes down to four levers: quality, latency, context window, and cost. For RAG specifically, prioritize context-following and citation behavior over raw benchmark scores.

# Technique 9: LLM Generation
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI

llm = ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-4o-mini", temperature=0.0, max_tokens=300)

# Pass the prompt string from Technique 8, not a dict.
response = llm.invoke(prompt)
print(response.content)

The four configuration knobs that matter:

  • Temperature (0.0 to 0.3 for factual Q&A). Higher temperature means more creative answers and more hallucination. For RAG, you want low.
  • Max tokens (cap aggressively). Prevents runaway responses and controls cost. Set based on what your channel can actually display.
  • Stop sequences. Useful for enforcing structured output formats. Stop on “Question:” if you do not want the model to continue past one answer.
  • System prompt. Reinforce grounding and citation requirements here, not in the user prompt. The system prompt has more authority in most models.

A trap I have watched teams fall into: picking a small encoder-decoder model like T5-large because it is “fine for retrieval QA.” T5-large has a 512-token context limit and will silently truncate long RAG contexts. Use a model with a real context window for any serious RAG work.

15. Post-processing and Response Delivery

The raw LLM output gets one more pass before it reaches the user.

# Technique 10: Post-processing
answer = response.content

# Simple grounding check: does the answer reuse context tokens?
context_tokens = set(context.lower().split())
answer_tokens = set(answer.lower().split())
overlap = len(answer_tokens & context_tokens) / max(len(answer_tokens), 1)

if overlap < 0.1:
    answer += "

[Low grounding confidence. Please verify.]"

print(answer)

What to do at the post-processing stage:

  • Format citations. Inline, footer, or clickable links. Pick a style and stay consistent across the product.
  • Truncate or summarize if too long. A 2,000-token answer that gets cut off by the UI is worse than a 500-token answer that fits.
  • Score or flag low-confidence responses. Even a dumb token-overlap heuristic catches obvious drift from the retrieved context.
  • Validate against retrieved context. For high-stakes domains, run a proper faithfulness scorer (covered in the next section) before delivery.

The final answer goes back through the original channel, whether that is a chat UI, an API response, an email, or a voice TTS pipeline.

16. Monitoring, Evaluation, and Human-in-the-Loop

This is the section most teams skip and later regret. RAG quality is not a one-time number you measure at launch. It drifts. Embeddings shift. Documents update. User queries change. If you are not measuring continuously, you are flying blind.

# Technique 11: RAGAS Evaluation
from datasets import Dataset
from ragas import evaluate

data = {
    "question": ["What is the return policy for Product X?"],
    "answer": ["Product X can be returned within 30 days with a receipt."],
    "contexts": [["Returns Policy, Section 4.1", "FAQ - Returns"]],
}
dataset = Dataset.from_dict(data)
result = evaluate(dataset)

# Example output shape. Actual scores depend entirely on your data. [ILLUSTRATIVE]
# {'context_precision': 0.75, 'faithfulness': 0.50, 'answer_relevancy': 0.80}
print(result)

The metrics split into three groups:

  • Retrieval metrics. Recall@K, Precision@K, MRR, and nDCG. These tell you whether you are finding the right chunks at all.
  • Generation metrics. Faithfulness, answer relevance, and citation correctness [7]. These tell you whether the model is using the chunks well.
  • End-to-end metrics. Task accuracy, user satisfaction, and latency. These tell you whether the whole system is delivering value.

The frameworks worth knowing:

  • RAGAS. Automated RAG evaluation across faithfulness, context precision, and answer relevance [7].
  • TruLens. Grounded feedback with detailed traces. Strong for debugging individual queries.
  • RAGChecker. Fine-grained diagnosis that pinpoints whether failures come from retrieval or generation [8].
  • OpenAI Evals. General LLM evaluation framework. Useful for custom eval criteria.
  • Evidently. Production monitoring with drift detection. Best for catching regressions after launch.

The single biggest mistake I see is treating evaluation as a launch checklist rather than an ongoing process. Run your eval suite on every prompt change. Run it on every embedding model upgrade. Run it weekly on production traffic samples. The goal is to catch regressions before users do.

17. Security, Privacy, and Compliance

Three risks live in this section. Prompt injection, where a malicious input convinces the model to ignore its instructions [10]. Data leakage, where the model echoes back something it should not have access to. RAG poisoning, where a malicious document enters your vector store and gets retrieved into someone else’s prompt.

# Technique 12: Basic injection detection
import re

INJECTION_PATTERNS = [
    r"ignore (all |previous )?instructions",
    r"system prompt",
    r"you are now",
]

def looks_like_injection(text: str) -> bool:
    lowered = text.lower()
    return any(re.search(p, lowered) for p in INJECTION_PATTERNS)

if looks_like_injection(query):
    raise ValueError("Potential prompt injection detected.")

The defenses worth running:

  • Sanitize all user and external inputs. Strip suspicious patterns, validate length, and reject queries that look like obvious attacks.
  • Validate outputs for leakage or unsafe content. A second LLM pass or a rule-based filter catches answers that include PII or violate content policies.
  • Implement role-based access control on retrieval. A user should only retrieve chunks they are allowed to see. This is where most teams cut corners and later regret it.
  • Redact PII and PHI at ingestion, not at output. Once sensitive data is in the vector store, it can leak through similarity search. Redact early.
  • Maintain audit logs for provenance. When something goes wrong, you need to reconstruct what got retrieved and what got generated. No logs, no audit.

Compliance matters even when nobody is asking yet. If you are handling healthcare data, financial data, or anything covered by GDPR or CCPA, the access controls and audit logs are not optional. The pattern-matching approach above catches obvious attacks. Sophisticated injection requires a classifier-based detector, which I covered in Pattern 4 of my production AI patterns article. Most tutorials skip security entirely, which is exactly why including it signals senior-level thinking to anyone reviewing your work.

18. Personalization and User Context

A premium customer asking about returns should retrieve premium-specific policy chunks, not the generic ones. A French-speaking user should get French-language responses. A user in the EU should not have their data leave the EU.

Example: “What is the return policy for Product X for premium customers?” triggers retrieval of premium-specific policies.

# Technique 13: Personalization
def personalize(query: str, user: dict) -> str:
    tier = user.get("tier", "standard")
    return f"[customer_tier={tier}] {query}"

personalized = personalize(query, {"tier": "premium"})

Three places to plug personalization into the pipeline:

  • Augment the query. Add profile data, order history, or preferences to the query before retrieval. A premium customer asking about returns gets a different query than a basic customer asking the same thing.
  • Filter retrieval by user role. A basic-tier user should not retrieve premium-tier policy chunks. Implement this as a metadata filter at the vector store level, not as a post-retrieval filter.
  • Adapt the prompt template. Tone, language, and region all live in the prompt. Different user segments deserve different prompts, not just different retrievals.

The trap to avoid: personalization that leaks across users. If your retrieval filter is wrong, a basic-tier user can accidentally retrieve premium-tier policy chunks, which is at best confusing and at worst a contract violation. Test the filtering as carefully as you test the retrieval.

19. Scaling, Performance, and Cost Optimization

RAG cost has three main drivers. Retrieval depth, reranking, and LLM call size. Each one is a tunable knob. The mistake is tuning them in isolation rather than against your latency and cost budget as a whole.

# Technique 14: Caching embeddings
from functools import lru_cache

@lru_cache(maxsize=2048)
def cached_embed(text: str):
    return tuple(model.encode(text).tolist())

Performance tactics that actually move the needle:

  • Shard the vector store for large corpora. Each shard fits in memory, parallel queries do not serialize, and you get linear scaling. The cost is operational complexity, which is real but manageable.
  • Batch and cache frequent queries. Embedding generation is expensive and highly cacheable. LRU caching at the query level is one of the highest-ROI optimizations in the entire pipeline.
  • Memory-map large indexes. Use mmap so you do not pay full RAM cost for indexes that exceed available memory.
  • Distributed cache for hot data. Redis or memcached for hot query results. A repeated user query should skip embedding, retrieval, and the LLM call entirely.

The cost trade-off in three knobs: retrieval depth (K), reranking (yes/no, how many candidates), and LLM call size (input plus output tokens). Tune all three together against your latency and cost budget, not in isolation. The single biggest cost win I have seen in production is caching at the right layer.

20. Fallback Strategies and Hybrid Systems

Not every query needs the full RAG pipeline. Some queries have a single right answer that you already know. “What is your refund policy?” Most companies have one canonical answer to this. Running it through retrieval and generation every time is wasteful and risks the model adding hallucinated details to a perfectly fine pre-written answer.

# Technique 15: FAQ Fallback
FAQ = {
    "what is the return policy": "Returns accepted within 30 days with receipt.",
}

def answer(query: str) -> str:
    key = normalize_query(query)
    for faq_q, faq_a in FAQ.items():
        if faq_q in key:
            return faq_a
    return run_rag_pipeline(query)  # defined elsewhere

The three-tier fallback pattern:

  • Tier 1: Hard-coded FAQ for high-frequency questions. Fast, accurate, deterministic. The right choice when you have a canonical answer that does not need to vary.
  • Tier 2: RAG for long-tail or novel queries. This is the bulk of your traffic. Retrieval and generation handle the questions that the FAQ does not cover.
  • Tier 3: Agentic flows for complex, multi-step tasks [6]. The LLM decides when to call tools, when to retrieve again, and when to escalate to a human.

The FAQ layer needs maintenance discipline. Stale FAQs are worse than no FAQs because users assume a hardcoded answer is the official answer. Build a regular review process and treat the FAQ as part of your content lifecycle, not a one-time setup.

21. Explainability, Provenance, and Auditability

Citations are not a nice-to-have feature. They are the difference between a system users trust and one they second-guess.

# Technique 16: Citation formatting
def format_citation(meta: dict) -> str:
    return (
        f"[Source: {meta['document']}, "
        f"Section {meta['section']}, "
        f"updated {meta['updated']}]"
    )

print(format_citation({
    "document": "Returns Policy",
    "section": "4.1",
    "updated": "2026-01-15",
}))

What to track and surface:

  • Source document, section, and version. Every retrieved chunk should carry this metadata. Without it, you cannot explain where an answer came from.
  • Inline citations or footnotes. Pick a format and use it consistently. Clickable links work best for web UIs. Footnote-style works for chat.
  • Audit logs for every retrieval and generation. When something goes wrong, you need to reconstruct what happened. Logs are the only way.

Example output:

The return period is 30 days for Product X. [Source: Returns Policy, Section 4.1, updated 2026–01–15]

The second-order benefit of forcing citations is that it makes hallucinations much easier to detect. If the model produces a fact with no citation, that fact is unverified. If it produces a citation that does not match the actual source content, you have a clear audit trail to follow. Citations are how you build a system you can actually trust in production.

22. Orchestration and Workflow Tooling

The frameworks that wire the stages together: LangChain, LlamaIndex, CrewAI. They manage the flow between ingestion, retrieval, reranking, prompt assembly, generation, and post-processing.

What the orchestration layer gives you:

  • Composable pipelines. Plug stages together without rebuilding glue code every time. Useful when your retrieval strategy changes mid-project.
  • Multi-agent coordination. Pattern multiple specialized agents (retrievers, planners, evaluators) into a workflow.
  • Observability hooks. Logging, tracing, and metrics at every stage. Essential for debugging production issues.
  • External tool integration. Connect to APIs, databases, and custom functions without writing new adapters every time.

Agentic RAG is the more flexible pattern, where the LLM itself decides when and how to retrieve, validate, and generate [6]. Instead of a fixed pipeline, the model can choose to retrieve again if its first results were thin, or skip retrieval entirely if it already has enough context. The flexibility comes at the cost of unpredictable latency and harder debugging.

For the architectural choices behind agentic flows and when MCP is the right primitive over plain RAG, see RAG vs MCP: The Architectural Difference Every AI Developer Must Understand.

The honest take on orchestration: start with the simplest fixed pipeline that solves your problem. Add agentic behavior only when you have a real reason. Most production systems do not need agentic flows, and the ones that do usually fail in subtler ways because of the added complexity.

23. End-to-End Code Example

Putting it all together. This is the skeleton of a working RAG system. Plug in your own documents, your own embedding model, and your own LLM, and you have a starting point.

from langchain_community.embeddings import HuggingFaceEmbeddings
from langchain_community.vectorstores import FAISS
from langchain.text_splitters import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter
from langchain_community.document_loaders import PyPDFLoader
from langchain.prompts import PromptTemplate
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI

# 1. Ingest and chunk documents
pdf_loader = PyPDFLoader("policy.pdf")
raw_docs = pdf_loader.load()
splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(chunk_size=500, chunk_overlap=100)
chunks = splitter.split_documents(raw_docs)

# 2. Embed and index
embeddings = HuggingFaceEmbeddings(model_name="sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
vectorstore = FAISS.from_documents(chunks, embeddings)

# 3. Retrieve
query = "What is the return policy for Product X?"
retrieved_docs = vectorstore.similarity_search(query, k=3)

# 4. Prompt construction
context = "

".join([doc.page_content for doc in retrieved_docs])
prompt = f"""
You are a helpful assistant. Use only the following context to answer the question.
Cite your sources.

Context:
{context}

Question: {query}
Answer:
"""

# 5. Generate answer
llm = ChatOpenAI(model_name="gpt-4o-mini")
response = llm.invoke({"user_question": query, "context": context})
print(response)

This is the minimum viable RAG system. It will work. It will not be great. Every section above shows you what to add next.

24. Conclusion: RAG in Practice

RAG is not magic and it is not dead. It is a pipeline of independently tunable components, each of which can quietly break your system if you ignore it. The model is rarely the problem. The pipeline almost always is.

The teams I have watched ship RAG systems that actually hold up under real users share three habits:

  • They treat every stage as a separate engineering surface, with its own tests and its own metrics.
  • They evaluate continuously, not just at launch. Drift is real. Documents change. Queries shift. Catching regressions early is cheaper than catching them in production.
  • They invest in the unglamorous parts. Ingestion, security, provenance, monitoring. The places where most teams skip steps and later regret it.

If your RAG is underperforming, work this list from the top. Most of the time, the fix is not a bigger model. It is a normalization step you skipped, a chunk size you never tuned, a reranker you never added, or a citation requirement you never enforced.

The model is doing its best. Give it a better pipeline.

Before You Go

If this saved you a RAG debugging session:

  • 👏 Clap if a technique made you rethink something
  • 💬 Comment with the technique you are implementing first
  • 🔗 Forward to a colleague building production RAG
  • ➕ Follow me on Medium for one production-AI deep dive each week

Further Reading

  • RAG vs MCP: The Architectural Difference Every AI Developer Must Understand
  • Stop Picking Between Vector and Graph: Real Production AI Needs Three Databases
  • Chunking Strategies in RAG Systems: Insights from 80+ GenAI Interviews
  • The 10 Questions That Decide Whether You’re an AI Engineer or Just an AI User
  • 11 Production AI Patterns Senior Engineers Are Quietly Adopting in 2026 (Part 1)

References

[2] Izacard and Grave, Leveraging Passage Retrieval with Generative Models for Open Domain QA, ICLR 2021 (FiD).

[3] Gao et al., Precise Zero-Shot Dense Retrieval without Relevance Labels, 2022 (HyDE).

[4] Rackauckas et al., RAG-Fusion: A New Take on Retrieval-Augmented Generation, arXiv 2024.

[5] Chen et al., RE-RAG: Reranking Enhanced RAG, EMNLP 2024.

[6] Asai et al., Self-RAG: Self-Reflective Retrieval-Augmented Generation, ICLR 2024.

[7] Es et al., RAGAS: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation, arXiv 2023.

[8] Ru et al., RAGChecker: A Fine-grained Framework for Diagnosing Retrieval-Augmented Generation, NeurIPS 2024.

item.title: Delegates and Events in iOS: The Concept That Finally Made App Communication Click for Me
item.content:encoded:
When I first started learning iOS development, delegates confused me more than I expected. The code itself did not look too hard. You create a protocol, add a delegate property, set it somewhere else, and call a method when something happens. But for a long time, I did not fully understand why this pattern existed or when I should use it instead of closures, NotificationCenter, SwiftUI state, or just calling another object directly.

That is one of the reasons I have been writing more iOS articles recently. I use these articles to track the issues I personally faced while building apps, especially the concepts that seemed simple at first but became more important as the app grew. I like documenting these lessons because if I struggled with something, there is a good chance someone else will run into the same confusion too. Hopefully, by sharing the mistakes and patterns that helped me, other developers can avoid repeating the same issues and get to the “aha” moment faster.

In some of my previous articles, I wrote about practical iOS topics from a similar angle. In SwiftUI State in iOS: A Practical Guide, I talked about how state drives the UI and why understanding state makes SwiftUI much easier to reason about. In MVVM in SwiftUI: Build an iOS App That Stays Organized as It Grows, I focused on keeping code organized when an app starts becoming more than just a few screens. I also wrote about trying Apple VisionKit and building a simple document scanner in SwiftUI, which was a good reminder that even in SwiftUI, many Apple frameworks still rely heavily on delegate-based APIs.

This article is about delegates and events in iOS. More importantly, it is about how objects communicate with each other without everything becoming tightly coupled and messy.

The Real Problem Delegates Solve

Before talking about delegates, it helps to understand the problem they are solving. Imagine we have a screen that displays a list of notes. When the user taps a note, we want to open the detail screen. The easiest way is to make the list screen directly call the detail screen.

final class NotesListViewController: UIViewController {

    private let detailViewController = NoteDetailViewController()

    func userDidTapNote(_ note: Note) {
        detailViewController.show(note)
    }
}

This works, and honestly, in a very small app it might feel completely fine. But the problem is that NotesListViewControllernow knows too much. It knows who handles the selected note, how the next screen works, and what should happen after the tap. That is okay when the app has two screens, but it starts becoming painful when the app grows.

What if tapping a note sometimes opens a detail screen, sometimes triggers an edit flow, and sometimes just informs a parent coordinator? What if this list component should be reused somewhere else? What if we want to track analytics when a note is selected, but we do not want the list view controller to know anything about analytics? This is where delegates become useful because they allow an object to say, “Something happened here,” without needing to know exactly who is handling it or what happens next.

A delegate is basically a way for one object to communicate events to another object through a clearly defined contract. In Swift, that contract is usually a protocol.

struct Note {
    let id: Int
    let title: String
}

protocol NotesListViewControllerDelegate: AnyObject {
    func notesListViewController(
        _ controller: NotesListViewController,
        didSelect note: Note
    )
}

Now the list screen can expose a delegate property.

final class NotesListViewController: UIViewController {

    weak var delegate: NotesListViewControllerDelegate?

    private let notes: [Note] = [
        Note(id: 1, title: "SwiftUI State"),
        Note(id: 2, title: "MVVM"),
        Note(id: 3, title: "Delegates and Events")
    ]

    func userDidTapNote(at index: Int) {
        let selectedNote = notes[index]

        delegate?.notesListViewController(
            self,
            didSelect: selectedNote
        )
    }
}

The important part here is that NotesListViewController does not decide what happens after the note is selected. It simply reports the event. Another object can become the delegate and decide what to do.

final class NotesCoordinator: NotesListViewControllerDelegate {

    func notesListViewController(
        _ controller: NotesListViewController,
        didSelect note: Note
    ) {
        print("User selected note: \(note.title)")

        // Open detail screen
        // Track analytics
        // Update app state
        // Start another flow
    }
}

This is the part that finally made delegates click for me. A delegate is not just extra syntax. It is a way to keep one object reusable and focused while letting another object handle the decision-making.

Why Delegates Are Usually Weak

One thing you will see a lot in delegate-based code is this:

weak var delegate: NotesListViewControllerDelegate?

At first, this can feel like one of those Swift details that people mention without explaining properly. But it matters because delegates often point back to an object that already owns the original object. For example, a parent view controller may own a child view controller, and then the child view controller may use the parent as its delegate.

final class ParentViewController: UIViewController {

    private let notesListViewController = NotesListViewController()

    override func viewDidLoad() {
        super.viewDidLoad()

        notesListViewController.delegate = self
    }
}

extension ParentViewController: NotesListViewControllerDelegate {

    func notesListViewController(
        _ controller: NotesListViewController,
        didSelect note: Note
    ) {
        print("Selected note: \(note.title)")
    }
}

If the parent strongly owns the child, and the child strongly owns the parent through the delegate, both objects can keep each other alive. That is called a retain cycle. To avoid this, delegate references are usually weak.

For a delegate to be weak, the protocol needs to be limited to class types. That is why we write AnyObject in the protocol declaration.

protocol NotesListViewControllerDelegate: AnyObject {
    func notesListViewController(
        _ controller: NotesListViewController,
        didSelect note: Note
    )
}

This is a small detail, but it is one of those details that becomes very important in real apps. If a view controller is not getting released from memory, a strong delegate reference is one of the first things I would check.

A Practical UIKit Example

Let’s use a more realistic example. Imagine we are building a reusable rating view. It shows buttons from 1 to 5, and when the user selects a rating, the parent screen needs to know. The rating view itself should not save the rating, call an API, show an alert, or navigate anywhere. Its job is only to display the buttons and report what the user selected.

First, we define the delegate protocol.

protocol RatingViewDelegate: AnyObject {
    func ratingView(_ ratingView: RatingView, didSelectRating rating: Int)
}

Now we can create the custom view.

import UIKit

final class RatingView: UIView {

    weak var delegate: RatingViewDelegate?

    private let stackView = UIStackView()

    override init(frame: CGRect) {
        super.init(frame: frame)
        setupView()
        setupButtons()
    }

    required init?(coder: NSCoder) {
        super.init(coder: coder)
        setupView()
        setupButtons()
    }

    private func setupView() {
        stackView.axis = .horizontal
        stackView.spacing = 8
        stackView.distribution = .fillEqually

        addSubview(stackView)
        stackView.translatesAutoresizingMaskIntoConstraints = false

        NSLayoutConstraint.activate([
            stackView.leadingAnchor.constraint(equalTo: leadingAnchor),
            stackView.trailingAnchor.constraint(equalTo: trailingAnchor),
            stackView.topAnchor.constraint(equalTo: topAnchor),
            stackView.bottomAnchor.constraint(equalTo: bottomAnchor)
        ])
    }

    private func setupButtons() {
        for rating in 1...5 {
            let button = UIButton(type: .system)
            button.setTitle("\(rating)", for: .normal)
            button.tag = rating

            button.addTarget(
                self,
                action: #selector(ratingButtonTapped(_:)),
                for: .touchUpInside
            )

            stackView.addArrangedSubview(button)
        }
    }

    @objc private func ratingButtonTapped(_ sender: UIButton) {
        let rating = sender.tag
        delegate?.ratingView(self, didSelectRating: rating)
    }
}

Then a view controller can use this rating view and decide what should happen when the rating is selected.

final class ReviewViewController: UIViewController {

    private let ratingView = RatingView()

    override func viewDidLoad() {
        super.viewDidLoad()

        view.backgroundColor = .systemBackground
        ratingView.delegate = self

        view.addSubview(ratingView)
        ratingView.translatesAutoresizingMaskIntoConstraints = false

        NSLayoutConstraint.activate([
            ratingView.centerXAnchor.constraint(equalTo: view.centerXAnchor),
            ratingView.centerYAnchor.constraint(equalTo: view.centerYAnchor),
            ratingView.widthAnchor.constraint(equalToConstant: 250),
            ratingView.heightAnchor.constraint(equalToConstant: 44)
        ])
    }
}

extension ReviewViewController: RatingViewDelegate {

    func ratingView(_ ratingView: RatingView, didSelectRating rating: Int) {
        print("Selected rating: \(rating)")

        // Save rating
        // Update UI
        // Send event to ViewModel
        // Track analytics
    }
}

This is a clean separation of responsibility. The RatingView only knows that a rating was tapped. The ReviewViewControllerdecides what that rating means in the context of the screen. This is the kind of separation that feels unnecessary in tiny examples, but becomes very valuable when you are building real screens that keep changing over time.

Delegates and Events Are Related, But Not Exactly the Same

An event is simply something that happened. A button was tapped. A text field changed. A scroll view moved. A network request finished. A document scanner completed scanning. A Bluetooth device disconnected. iOS apps are basically a long chain of events being handled in different ways.

Delegates are one way to handle events, but they are not the only way. UIKit and Swift give us several patterns, and this is where things can get confusing. You might see target-action for button taps, delegates for table views, closures for small callbacks, NotificationCenter for broadcasts, Combine publishers for streams, and SwiftUI modifiers like .onAppear and .onChange.

// Target-action
button.addTarget(
    self,
    action: #selector(buttonTapped),
    for: .touchUpInside
)

// Delegate
tableView.delegate = self

// Closure callback
view.onRetryTapped = { [weak self] in
    self?.reloadData()
}

// NotificationCenter
NotificationCenter.default.post(
    name: .userDidLogout,
    object: nil
)

// SwiftUI event modifier
.onAppear {
    loadData()
}

The trick is not to memorize every pattern as a separate thing. The better mental model is to ask: who needs to know that this happened, and how closely related are these objects? Once you answer that, the right pattern usually becomes easier to choose.

Target-Action Is Great for Simple UI Events

Target-action is very common in UIKit, especially with controls like UIButton, UISwitch, UISlider, and UITextField. If a user taps a button, you usually do not need a delegate protocol just for that one tap. Target-action is simple and direct.

final class LoginViewController: UIViewController {

    private let loginButton = UIButton(type: .system)

    override func viewDidLoad() {
        super.viewDidLoad()

        loginButton.setTitle("Login", for: .normal)

        loginButton.addTarget(
            self,
            action: #selector(loginButtonTapped),
            for: .touchUpInside
        )
    }

    @objc private func loginButtonTapped() {
        print("Login button tapped")
    }
}

This is perfect for simple UI interactions. The button sends an event, and the view controller handles it. You will commonly see events like .touchUpInside, .editingChanged, .valueChanged, and .primaryActionTriggered.

textField.addTarget(
    self,
    action: #selector(textDidChange(_:)),
    for: .editingChanged
)

switchControl.addTarget(
    self,
    action: #selector(switchValueChanged(_:)),
    for: .valueChanged
)

My rule is simple: if it is a direct UIKit control event, target-action is usually fine. I only start thinking about delegates or closures when I am building a custom component or when the communication becomes more structured.

Delegates Are Better for Structured Communication

Delegates are especially useful when one object needs to communicate multiple related events or decisions to another object. This is why UITableViewDelegate, UITableViewDataSource, UITextFieldDelegate, UIScrollViewDelegate, and many Apple framework APIs use delegates.

Take UITableView as an example. A table view does not only need to say “a row was tapped.” It may also need to ask how many rows exist, what each cell should look like, how tall a row should be, whether a row can be edited, and what should happen when a row is selected.

final class NotesViewController: UIViewController {

    private let tableView = UITableView()
    private let notes = ["SwiftUI State", "MVVM", "Delegates"]

    override func viewDidLoad() {
        super.viewDidLoad()

        tableView.dataSource = self
        tableView.delegate = self
    }
}

extension NotesViewController: UITableViewDataSource {

    func tableView(
        _ tableView: UITableView,
        numberOfRowsInSection section: Int
    ) -> Int {
        notes.count
    }

    func tableView(
        _ tableView: UITableView,
        cellForRowAt indexPath: IndexPath
    ) -> UITableViewCell {
        let cell = UITableViewCell(style: .default, reuseIdentifier: nil)
        cell.textLabel?.text = notes[indexPath.row]
        return cell
    }
}

extension NotesViewController: UITableViewDelegate {

    func tableView(
        _ tableView: UITableView,
        didSelectRowAt indexPath: IndexPath
    ) {
        print("Selected note: \(notes[indexPath.row])")
    }
}

This is where delegates shine. The table view has a clear relationship with the object that manages it. The delegate and data source define that relationship in a structured way. This is much cleaner than giving the table view many random closures for every possible behavior.

UITextFieldDelegate is another good example because the text field sometimes needs to ask questions before doing something.

final class ProfileViewController: UIViewController {

    private let nameTextField = UITextField()

    override func viewDidLoad() {
        super.viewDidLoad()

        nameTextField.delegate = self
    }
}

extension ProfileViewController: UITextFieldDelegate {

    func textFieldShouldReturn(_ textField: UITextField) -> Bool {
        textField.resignFirstResponder()
        return true
    }

    func textFieldDidEndEditing(_ textField: UITextField) {
        print("User entered name: \(textField.text ?? "")")
    }
}

This is not just an event callback. The text field is asking the delegate how it should behave. That is another reason delegates are useful: they are not only for reporting events, but also for letting another object customize behavior.

Closures Are Great for Small Custom Events

While delegates are useful, I do not think every custom view needs a delegate. Sometimes a closure is simpler and more readable. For example, imagine we have an empty state view with a retry button. If the only thing the view needs to report is “retry was tapped,” a closure works nicely.

final class EmptyStateView: UIView {

    var onRetryTapped: (() -> Void)?

    private let retryButton = UIButton(type: .system)

    override init(frame: CGRect) {
        super.init(frame: frame)
        setupButton()
    }

    required init?(coder: NSCoder) {
        super.init(coder: coder)
        setupButton()
    }

    private func setupButton() {
        retryButton.setTitle("Try Again", for: .normal)

        retryButton.addTarget(
            self,
            action: #selector(retryButtonTapped),
            for: .touchUpInside
        )

        addSubview(retryButton)
    }

    @objc private func retryButtonTapped() {
        onRetryTapped?()
    }
}

Then the view controller can handle the callback like this:

final class ErrorViewController: UIViewController {

    private let emptyStateView = EmptyStateView()

    override func viewDidLoad() {
        super.viewDidLoad()

        emptyStateView.onRetryTapped = { [weak self] in
            self?.reloadData()
        }
    }

    private func reloadData() {
        print("Reloading data...")
    }
}

The important thing with closures is memory management. If a view owns a closure, and that closure strongly captures the view controller, you can accidentally create a retain cycle. That is why you often see [weak self] inside UIKit callbacks.

emptyStateView.onRetryTapped = { [weak self] in
    self?.reloadData()
}

My personal rule is that closures are great when there are one or two simple events. If the custom view starts exposing many callbacks, I usually move to a delegate because the API becomes easier to organize and understand.

NotificationCenter Is for Broadcast Events

NotificationCenter is another event pattern, but I try to use it carefully. It is useful when multiple unrelated parts of the app need to know about the same event. A common example is logout. When the user logs out, the profile screen may need to reset, the root screen may need to return to login, cached data may need to clear, and other parts of the app may need to react.

First, define a notification name.

extension Notification.Name {
    static let userDidLogout = Notification.Name("userDidLogout")
}

Then post the event when logout happens.

final class SessionManager {

    func logout() {
        // Clear tokens
        // Reset user session
        // Remove cached data

        NotificationCenter.default.post(
            name: .userDidLogout,
            object: nil
        )
    }
}

Any object that cares about logout can listen for it.

final class HomeViewController: UIViewController {

    override func viewDidLoad() {
        super.viewDidLoad()

        NotificationCenter.default.addObserver(
            self,
            selector: #selector(handleLogout),
            name: .userDidLogout,
            object: nil
        )
    }

    @objc private func handleLogout() {
        print("User logged out. Return to login screen.")
    }

    deinit {
        NotificationCenter.default.removeObserver(self)
    }
}

This is powerful, but it can also make the app harder to trace if overused. With delegates, you can usually see the relationship clearly. With notifications, the event is broadcast, and any object can listen from anywhere. That is useful for app-wide events, but I would not use it for every button tap or small component callback.

SwiftUI Handles Events Differently

In SwiftUI, we usually do not write delegates for basic view interactions. SwiftUI gives us event-style modifiers and closures instead. A button tap is just a closure.

struct LoginView: View {

    var body: some View {
        Button("Login") {
            print("Login tapped")
        }
    }
}

Text changes can be handled with .onChange.

struct SearchView: View {

    @State private var searchText = ""

    var body: some View {
        TextField("Search", text: $searchText)
            .onChange(of: searchText) { oldValue, newValue in
                print("Search changed to: \(newValue)")
            }
    }
}

View lifecycle events can be handled with .onAppear and .onDisappear.

struct ProfileView: View {

    var body: some View {
        Text("Profile")
            .onAppear {
                print("Profile appeared")
            }
            .onDisappear {
                print("Profile disappeared")
            }
    }
}

This connects nicely with the SwiftUI state idea. In UIKit, we often think, “When this event happens, update this label or push this screen.” In SwiftUI, we usually think, “When this event happens, update the state, and the UI will reflect that state.”

struct LoginFormView: View {

    @State private var email = ""
    @State private var password = ""
    @State private var errorMessage: String?

    var body: some View {
        VStack(spacing: 12) {
            TextField("Email", text: $email)
                .textFieldStyle(.roundedBorder)

            SecureField("Password", text: $password)
                .textFieldStyle(.roundedBorder)

            Button("Login") {
                login()
            }

            if let errorMessage {
                Text(errorMessage)
                    .foregroundStyle(.red)
            }
        }
        .padding()
    }

    private func login() {
        guard !email.isEmpty else {
            errorMessage = "Email is required"
            return
        }

        guard !password.isEmpty else {
            errorMessage = "Password is required"
            return
        }

        errorMessage = nil
        print("Perform login")
    }
}

Here, the button tap is the event, and errorMessage is the state. Once the state changes, SwiftUI updates the UI. This is why understanding events and state together is so helpful.

Bridging UIKit Delegates Into SwiftUI

Even if you are mainly writing SwiftUI, delegates still matter because many Apple frameworks are built around them. UIImagePickerController, VNDocumentCameraViewController, CLLocationManager, CBCentralManager, WKWebView, and many other APIs use delegates. This is exactly why delegates came back into the picture when I was working with VisionKit.

When you wrap UIKit inside SwiftUI, you usually use UIViewControllerRepresentable or UIViewRepresentable. Since UIKit expects a delegate object, SwiftUI gives us a Coordinator to bridge that delegate communication back into SwiftUI.

Here is an example using UIImagePickerController.

import SwiftUI
import UIKit

struct ImagePicker: UIViewControllerRepresentable {

    @Binding var selectedImage: UIImage?
    @Environment(\.dismiss) private var dismiss

    func makeUIViewController(context: Context) -> UIImagePickerController {
        let picker = UIImagePickerController()
        picker.delegate = context.coordinator
        picker.sourceType = .photoLibrary
        return picker
    }

    func updateUIViewController(
        _ uiViewController: UIImagePickerController,
        context: Context
    ) {
        // No update needed for this example
    }

    func makeCoordinator() -> Coordinator {
        Coordinator(self)
    }

    final class Coordinator: NSObject,
                             UIImagePickerControllerDelegate,
                             UINavigationControllerDelegate {

        private let parent: ImagePicker

        init(_ parent: ImagePicker) {
            self.parent = parent
        }

        func imagePickerController(
            _ picker: UIImagePickerController,
            didFinishPickingMediaWithInfo info: [UIImagePickerController.InfoKey : Any]
        ) {
            if let image = info[.originalImage] as? UIImage {
                parent.selectedImage = image
            }

            parent.dismiss()
        }

        func imagePickerControllerDidCancel(_ picker: UIImagePickerController) {
            parent.dismiss()
        }
    }
}

Now the SwiftUI view can use the image picker with a binding.

struct ProfilePhotoView: View {

    @State private var selectedImage: UIImage?
    @State private var isShowingImagePicker = false

    var body: some View {
        VStack(spacing: 16) {
            if let selectedImage {
                Image(uiImage: selectedImage)
                    .resizable()
                    .scaledToFit()
                    .frame(height: 200)
            } else {
                Text("No image selected")
            }

            Button("Choose Photo") {
                isShowingImagePicker = true
            }
        }
        .sheet(isPresented: $isShowingImagePicker) {
            ImagePicker(selectedImage: $selectedImage)
        }
    }
}

This pattern is very common. UIKit reports events through a delegate. The coordinator receives those delegate events. Then the coordinator updates SwiftUI state through a binding. Once I understood this flow, wrapping UIKit controllers in SwiftUI became much less mysterious.

Delegate vs Closure: A Practical Decision

Let’s say we are building a reusable login form view in UIKit. The form has an email field, password field, login button, and forgot password button. We could expose two closures like this.

final class LoginFormView: UIView {

    var onLoginTapped: ((_ email: String, _ password: String) -> Void)?
    var onForgotPasswordTapped: (() -> Void)?

    private let emailTextField = UITextField()
    private let passwordTextField = UITextField()
    private let loginButton = UIButton(type: .system)
    private let forgotPasswordButton = UIButton(type: .system)

    override init(frame: CGRect) {
        super.init(frame: frame)
        setupActions()
    }

    required init?(coder: NSCoder) {
        super.init(coder: coder)
        setupActions()
    }

    private func setupActions() {
        loginButton.addTarget(
            self,
            action: #selector(loginButtonTapped),
            for: .touchUpInside
        )

        forgotPasswordButton.addTarget(
            self,
            action: #selector(forgotPasswordButtonTapped),
            for: .touchUpInside
        )
    }

    @objc private func loginButtonTapped() {
        onLoginTapped?(
            emailTextField.text ?? "",
            passwordTextField.text ?? ""
        )
    }

    @objc private func forgotPasswordButtonTapped() {
        onForgotPasswordTapped?()
    }
}

This is perfectly fine for a small component. But if the form starts growing with more related behavior, a delegate can make the API feel cleaner.

protocol LoginFormViewDelegate: AnyObject {
    func loginFormView(
        _ view: LoginFormView,
        didTapLoginWithEmail email: String,
        password: String
    )

    func loginFormViewDidTapForgotPassword(_ view: LoginFormView)
}

Then the form view can communicate through the delegate.

final class LoginFormView: UIView {

    weak var delegate: LoginFormViewDelegate?

    private let emailTextField = UITextField()
    private let passwordTextField = UITextField()
    private let loginButton = UIButton(type: .system)
    private let forgotPasswordButton = UIButton(type: .system)

    override init(frame: CGRect) {
        super.init(frame: frame)
        setupActions()
    }

    required init?(coder: NSCoder) {
        super.init(coder: coder)
        setupActions()
    }

    private func setupActions() {
        loginButton.addTarget(
            self,
            action: #selector(loginButtonTapped),
            for: .touchUpInside
        )

        forgotPasswordButton.addTarget(
            self,
            action: #selector(forgotPasswordButtonTapped),
            for: .touchUpInside
        )
    }

    @objc private func loginButtonTapped() {
        delegate?.loginFormView(
            self,
            didTapLoginWithEmail: emailTextField.text ?? "",
            password: passwordTextField.text ?? ""
        )
    }

    @objc private func forgotPasswordButtonTapped() {
        delegate?.loginFormViewDidTapForgotPassword(self)
    }
}

And the view controller handles the behavior.

final class LoginViewController: UIViewController {

    private let loginFormView = LoginFormView()
    private let viewModel = LoginViewModel()

    override func viewDidLoad() {
        super.viewDidLoad()

        loginFormView.delegate = self
    }
}

extension LoginViewController: LoginFormViewDelegate {

    func loginFormView(
        _ view: LoginFormView,
        didTapLoginWithEmail email: String,
        password: String
    ) {
        Task {
            do {
                try await viewModel.login(email: email, password: password)
                print("Navigate to home")
            } catch {
                print("Show error: \(error)")
            }
        }
    }

    func loginFormViewDidTapForgotPassword(_ view: LoginFormView) {
        print("Navigate to forgot password")
    }
}

The view model can stay focused on business logic.

final class LoginViewModel {

    func login(email: String, password: String) async throws {
        guard !email.isEmpty else {
            throw LoginError.missingEmail
        }

        guard !password.isEmpty else {
            throw LoginError.missingPassword
        }

        // Call login API here
    }
}

enum LoginError: Error {
    case missingEmail
    case missingPassword
}

This connects directly with MVVM. The view reports the event, the view controller receives it, and the view model handles the logic. The login form does not need to know about networking, navigation, alerts, or authentication rules. That separation is what keeps the code easier to change later.

Naming Delegate Methods Clearly

One thing I appreciate more now is good delegate method naming. Apple’s APIs usually follow a pattern that makes the method read almost like a sentence.

func tableView(
    _ tableView: UITableView,
    didSelectRowAt indexPath: IndexPath
)

That method name tells us which object triggered the event, what happened, and what extra information is being passed. I try to follow the same style in my own code.

func scannerViewController(
    _ controller: ScannerViewController,
    didFinishScanning pages: [UIImage]
)

func scannerViewControllerDidCancel(
    _ controller: ScannerViewController
)

func loginFormView(
    _ view: LoginFormView,
    didTapLoginWithEmail email: String,
    password: String
)

This may look verbose, but it helps a lot when the codebase grows. A vague method like login() or done() may look cleaner today, but six months later you may not remember who called it, why it was called, or what context it belongs to. Clear delegate names make the code easier to scan and easier to debug.

Common Mistakes I Try to Avoid Now

The first mistake is forgetting to set the delegate. This is such a simple mistake, but it can waste a lot of time because the app compiles and runs, but nothing happens when the event is triggered.

loginFormView.delegate = self

The second mistake is forgetting to make the delegate weak. This can cause memory leaks, especially when a child object points back to its parent. If the delegate is a class-based relationship, I usually expect to see weak.

weak var delegate: LoginFormViewDelegate?

The third mistake is using delegates for everything. Not every event needs a protocol. If it is a simple button tap inside a view controller, target-action is enough. If it is one small custom callback, a closure may be cleaner. If it is a SwiftUI interaction, state and closures are usually the natural choice.

The fourth mistake is letting a view do too much. A custom view should usually report user actions, not decide the entire app flow. For example, I would avoid putting API calls, navigation, analytics, and alert handling directly inside a reusable form view.

final class LoginFormView: UIView {

    @objc private func loginButtonTapped() {
        // This is too much responsibility for a reusable view.
        // Validate input
        // Call API
        // Navigate to home screen
        // Show alert
        // Track analytics
    }
}

A cleaner approach is to let the view report the event and let another layer decide what to do.

@objc private func loginButtonTapped() {
    delegate?.loginFormView(
        self,
        didTapLoginWithEmail: emailTextField.text ?? "",
        password: passwordTextField.text ?? ""
    )
}

This is a small shift in thinking, but it makes components much easier to reuse.

The Mental Model I Use Now

The easiest way I think about delegates and events is this: something happens in one object, and another object needs to know about it. That is really the core idea. The pattern you choose depends on the relationship between those objects.

If it is a simple UIKit control event, I use target-action. If it is one small custom callback, I usually use a closure. If it is a structured relationship with multiple related events, I use a delegate. If many unrelated parts of the app need to know about the same thing, I consider NotificationCenter. If I am in SwiftUI, I usually think in terms of closures, bindings, state, and modifiers like .onAppear, .onChange, and .task.

The question that helps me most is: “Who needs to know this happened?” If only the parent view needs to know, a closure or delegate may be enough. If the object needs to ask its owner multiple things, a delegate is probably better. If the whole app needs to react, a broadcast-style event may make sense.

Final Thoughts

Delegates can feel like an older iOS concept, especially when working with SwiftUI, async/await, and modern closure-based APIs. But they are still everywhere in iOS development. UIKit uses them heavily. Many Apple frameworks use them. SwiftUI wrappers often need coordinators because the UIKit controller underneath still communicates through delegates.

For me, the concept became much easier once I stopped thinking of delegates as just boilerplate. A delegate is simply a way for an object to say, “Something happened here, and I want someone else to decide what to do.” That is a powerful idea because it keeps objects focused, reusable, and less tightly connected.

I am continuing to write these iOS articles as a way to document the concepts and issues I run into while building apps. Some topics look simple in sample code, but they become much more meaningful when you start building real features. Delegates and events are exactly that kind of topic.

If this article helped you, please clap for it and follow me for more practical iOS development articles. It really helps and also motivates me to keep sharing what I learn while building.
